questions.question: RestTemplate vs WebClient vs Feign vs Spring 6 HTTP Interface — which HTTP client in 2026?
questions.title: RestTemplate vs WebClient vs Feign vs HTTP Interface
questions.direct_answer: In 2026, pick by model and async needs: **Spring 6 HTTP Interface** (`@HttpExchange`) is the modern default — declarative, works with `RestClient` (sync) or `WebClient` (reactive), minimal boilerplate, built-in. **WebClient** is the reactive/non-blocking client — use for high-concurrency or WebFlux apps. **`RestClient`** (Spring 6.1+) is the modern synchronous replacement for RestTemplate — fluent, built on top of same HTTP infra. **RestTemplate** is in maintenance mode — still supported, no new features, migrate away for new code. **OpenFeign** is still popular via Spring Cloud OpenFeign — declarative like HTTP Interface but external dep; use if you're already on Spring Cloud. **Default pick for new Spring 6+ code: `@HttpExchange` backed by `RestClient` for sync or `WebClient` for reactive.** Wrap with Resilience4j for circuit breaking, timeouts, retries; tune connection pool; propagate trace headers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Modern Spring HTTP client choice; resilience and observability
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using RestTemplate for new code; no timeouts; no connection pool tuning; no circuit breaker; blocking in WebFlux
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss @HttpExchange, Spring 6 RestClient, Project Loom virtual threads, Resilience4j integration, distributed tracing propagation

sections.title: The Java HTTP Client Landscape in 2026
sections.content:
Spring has quietly consolidated its HTTP clients over the past few releases. The 2026 picture:

**Spring 6 HTTP Interface (`@HttpExchange`)** — declarative interface-based client (since Spring 6). You define an interface; Spring generates the proxy. Backed by either `RestClient` (sync) or `WebClient` (reactive). Replaces much of the motivation for Feign in Spring-native apps.

**`RestClient`** (Spring 6.1+) — modern synchronous client with fluent API. Sits on top of the same infrastructure as `RestTemplate` and `WebClient`, but with better ergonomics. The recommended synchronous choice for new code.

**`WebClient`** (Spring 5+) — reactive, non-blocking.
- Used in WebFlux apps and whenever you want non-blocking I/O in Spring MVC.
- Supports streaming, SSE, async responses.
- With **Project Loom virtual threads**, the distinction 'need non-blocking' softens — Tomcat on Loom handles many blocking clients efficiently — but WebClient remains the right pick for streaming, heavy concurrency, or reactive pipelines.

**`RestTemplate`** — the legacy synchronous client. Still supported, still works; in **maintenance mode** (no new features since Spring 5). For new code, use `RestClient` or `@HttpExchange`.

**OpenFeign (Spring Cloud OpenFeign)** — declarative HTTP client from Netflix OSS / Spring Cloud.
- Similar to `@HttpExchange` conceptually but more mature, with richer plugin ecosystem (Hystrix/Resilience4j integration, request/response logging, custom encoders).
- Still widely used in Spring Cloud stacks.
- The case for Feign weakens in Spring 6+ with native `@HttpExchange`.

**Java 11+ `java.net.http.HttpClient`** — JDK-native HTTP/2 client. Low-level; fine for simple use. Spring clients generally wrap more operational concerns (instrumentation, observability, timeouts) on top.

**Apache HttpClient 5, OkHttp** — low-level HTTP libraries Spring can sit on top of (ClientHttpRequestFactory). Use for specific features (HTTP/2 fine-grained tuning, HTTP/3, connection pooling).

sections.title: Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | RestTemplate | RestClient | WebClient | @HttpExchange | OpenFeign |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Style** | Imperative, methods | Imperative, fluent | Reactive fluent | Declarative interface | Declarative interface |
| **Status** | Maintenance | Current default (sync) | Current default (reactive) | Current default (declarative) | Spring Cloud extension |
| **Thread model** | Blocking | Blocking | Non-blocking | Sync or reactive based on backing | Blocking by default |
| **Spring version** | 3.0+ | 6.1+ | 5.0+ | 6.0+ | Spring Cloud |
| **Backing HTTP lib** | JDK/Apache/OkHttp | Same | Reactor Netty default | Same as backing | Apache/OkHttp |
| **HTTP/2, streaming** | Limited | Yes via lib | Native | Via backing | Via lib |
| **Boilerplate** | Medium | Low (fluent) | Low-medium | Very low (declarative) | Very low (declarative) |
| **Resilience (CB, retry, timeout)** | Add separately | Add separately | Add separately | Add separately | Built-in (Hystrix/Resilience4j) |
| **Observability hooks** | Manual | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Best for** | Legacy maintenance | Modern sync | Reactive / streaming / high concurrency | New Spring 6+ code | Existing Spring Cloud stacks |

sections.title: Usage Examples
Production Concerns: Timeouts, Resilience, Observability
sections.content:
**Timeouts are non-negotiable.** Every HTTP call must have:
- **Connect timeout** (1–2s typical internal; 5s external)
- **Read timeout** (2–10s internal; 10–30s external)
- **Total / request timeout** (overall ceiling)

Default HTTP clients often have huge or no timeouts; requests hang forever.

**Connection pool tuning:**
- Default pool sizes rarely fit production
- Tune: max connections per route, total max, idle timeout, evict policy
- Monitor pool saturation

**Example with Apache HttpClient 5 + RestClient:**

```java
PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager cm = new PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager();
cm.setMaxTotal(200);
cm.setDefaultMaxPerRoute(50);

CloseableHttpClient http = HttpClients.custom()
    .setConnectionManager(cm)
    .setDefaultRequestConfig(RequestConfig.custom()
        .setConnectTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(2))
        .setResponseTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(5))
        .build())
    .build();

RestClient client = RestClient.builder()
    .requestFactory(new HttpComponentsClientHttpRequestFactory(http))
    .build();
```

**Circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, rate limiter — Resilience4j:**

```java
@Service
public class PaymentClient {

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
    @Retry(name = "payment")
    @Bulkhead(name = "payment", type = Bulkhead.Type.SEMAPHORE)
    @TimeLimiter(name = "payment")
    public CompletableFuture<ChargeResponse> charge(Charge c) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() ->
            restClient.post().uri("/charge").body(c)
                .retrieve().body(ChargeResponse.class));
    }

    public CompletableFuture<ChargeResponse> fallback(Charge c, Throwable t) {
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(ChargeResponse.deferred(c.id()));
    }
}
```

config in `application.yml`:

```yaml
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payment:
        slidingWindowSize: 20
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 10s
  retry:
    instances:
      payment:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 200ms
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      payment:
        timeoutDuration: 3s
```

**Observability:**

- **Metrics**: Micrometer auto-instruments `RestClient`, `WebClient`, `RestTemplate`; metrics include `http.client.requests` with URI, method, status, outcome
- **Tracing**: Spring + OpenTelemetry / Micrometer Tracing auto-propagates `traceparent` header; distributed traces include outbound calls
- **Logging**: carefully — don't log full request bodies (PII/secrets); log correlation id, URL, status, duration

**Auth propagation:**

- If call is on behalf of user, propagate JWT / auth context
- Service-to-service: use OAuth2 client credentials or mTLS
- `ExchangeFilterFunction` (WebClient), `RestClient` interceptors, or `RequestInterceptor` (Feign) to inject tokens

**MDC / tracing headers propagation:**

When switching threads (reactive, CompletableFuture, scheduled), MDC can be lost. Spring Cloud Sleuth / Micrometer Tracing handle propagation. Verify trace IDs appear in downstream service logs.

**Serialization:**

- Default Jackson config OK for most
- Configure `ObjectMapper` globally with `FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false`, date formats
- For gRPC-like perf, consider Protobuf over JSON; but REST + Jackson is the default

**Error handling patterns:**

- Don't let `RestClientException` bubble unfiltered; map to domain exceptions
- Distinguish 4xx (client error, don't retry), 5xx (server error, retry idempotent), 429 (rate limited, back off), 503 (service unavailable, retry)
- Idempotency keys on non-idempotent POSTs when retrying

sections.title: Trade-offs and Decision Guide
sections.content:
**RestTemplate in 2026**: fine for existing code; don't start new projects with it. Migrate when refactoring or when new features need modern client.

**RestClient vs WebClient — when sync vs reactive**:
- Sync (`RestClient`): simpler debugging, stack traces, Transactional boundaries
- Reactive (`WebClient`): non-blocking, streaming, high concurrency, backpressure
- With Project Loom (JDK 21+ virtual threads), sync Tomcat + RestClient handles high concurrency efficiently; reactive's pure concurrency advantage softens
- Still pick WebClient for streaming (SSE, chunked), fully reactive pipelines, or WebFlux apps

**@HttpExchange vs Feign**:
- `@HttpExchange` is native to Spring 6; no extra dep
- Feign has deeper ecosystem (Spring Cloud, LoadBalancer integration, decoders)
- New code on Spring 6+: `@HttpExchange` usually wins on simplicity
- Existing Spring Cloud projects: Feign is often entrenched; migrating is refactor work

**When NOT to use declarative (HTTP Interface/Feign)**:
- Complex dynamic URL building; computed headers per request; programmatic logic around the call
- Situations needing per-call `ExchangeFilterFunction` or interceptor
- Streaming with per-chunk logic
- Use imperative `RestClient` or `WebClient` directly

**Resilience patterns are essential**:
- Every external call should have timeout, retry (for idempotent), circuit breaker
- Resilience4j is the 2026 Java resilience library (Hystrix deprecated)
- Set per-client configs; defaults often too lenient

**Connection pooling mistakes**:
- No pool configured: default huge / unbounded; saturation easy
- Pool too small: requests queue; added latency
- Pool too large: server connection limits overwhelmed
- Monitor: active connections, leased, available, queue time

**HTTP/2 adoption**:
- WebClient (Reactor Netty) supports HTTP/2 well
- RestClient with JDK HttpClient supports HTTP/2
- Apache HttpClient 5 supports HTTP/2
- HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces connection overhead

**HTTP/3 (QUIC)**:
- Emerging; not universal Spring support yet
- JDK and Netty have experimental; production use niche

**gRPC as alternative**:
- For internal microservice calls, gRPC often better: HTTP/2, Protobuf, strong types, streaming
- Spring gRPC starter (grpc-spring-boot-starter) makes it easy
- REST still default for public APIs

**Circuit breaker antipattern**:
- Fallback that masks errors silently → user sees success when system failed
- Fallback should: return cached/default data, queue for later, clearly indicate failure mode
- Don't use circuit breaker to paper over bad dependencies; fix the dependency

**Retry antipattern**:
- Retrying non-idempotent POSTs without idempotency keys → duplicate actions
- Retrying on every exception (including client errors) → wastes capacity, DDoSes dependency
- Exponential backoff + jitter; cap attempts (3 typical)

**Timeout antipattern**:
- 30s default; requests hang; thread pool exhausts; cascading failure
- Set aggressive internal timeouts (2–5s)
- Timeout budget must account for retries; 3 retries of 5s = 15s total; caller upstream may give up

**Tracing propagation**:
- Verify `traceparent` / `X-B3-TraceId` headers flow through
- Datadog / Jaeger / Tempo should show cross-service spans
- Missing spans = instrumentation gap

**Testing HTTP clients**:
- **MockWebServer** (okhttp): full HTTP mock; great integration tests
- **WireMock**: classic Java HTTP mock
- **MockRestServiceServer** (Spring): mock-the-client side for unit-ish tests
- Use real HTTP mocks over mocking `RestTemplate` itself

**Security concerns**:
- TLS for all external calls (http⇒https)
- Validate certificates; don't disable verification in production
- mTLS for service-to-service (via Istio or manual)
- Secret management for API keys (Vault, Secrets Manager); never hardcoded
- Don't log credentials or bearer tokens

**Migration path:**
- RestTemplate → RestClient: mechanical; similar API shape
- RestTemplate → `@HttpExchange`: refactor to interface
- Feign → `@HttpExchange`: similar declarative style; check for Spring Cloud features used (LoadBalancer integration, custom encoders)
- Blocking client in reactive pipeline → WebClient

**Default recommendation for Spring 6+ new code:** 1.
- Define `@HttpExchange` interface for each remote service
2.
- Back with `RestClient` for sync (or `WebClient` for reactive/streaming)
3.
- Configure connect/read/overall timeouts
4.
- Tune connection pool (Apache HttpClient 5 or OkHttp)
5.
- Wrap with Resilience4j (CB, retry, timeout, bulkhead)
6. Propagate tracing and auth headers
7. Use Micrometer for metrics
8. Test with MockWebServer/WireMock

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Default for Spring 6+**: `@HttpExchange` interface + `RestClient` (sync) or `WebClient` (reactive)
- **RestTemplate in maintenance** — don't start new projects with it
- **WebClient** for reactive, streaming, high concurrency; Project Loom softens this
- **OpenFeign** still great in Spring Cloud stacks; `@HttpExchange` reduces need
- **Timeouts non-negotiable** — connect (1–2s), read (2–10s), overall ceiling
- **Connection pool tuning** mandatory; defaults unsuitable for production
- **Resilience4j** for circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, timeout — essential
- **Observability**: Micrometer metrics, distributed tracing, careful logging
- **Auth propagation**: bearer tokens via interceptor; mTLS for service-to-service
- **Test with MockWebServer / WireMock**; don't mock client objects directly

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In 2026, pick by model and async needs.

**Spring 6 HTTP Interface (@HttpExchange) is the modern default**
- Declarative interface-based
- Works with RestClient (sync) or WebClient (reactive)
- Minimal boilerplate; built-in to Spring 6+
- Reduces need for Feign in Spring-native apps

**RestClient (Spring 6.1+)**
- Modern synchronous replacement for RestTemplate
- Fluent API
- Built on same HTTP infra
- Recommended synchronous choice for new code

**WebClient**
- Reactive, non-blocking
- Used in WebFlux apps; whenever non-blocking I/O needed in Spring MVC
- Streaming, SSE, async responses
- With Project Loom virtual threads, the pure concurrency advantage softens; still right for streaming or fully reactive pipelines

**RestTemplate**
- Legacy synchronous; in maintenance mode
- No new features since Spring 5
- For new code, use RestClient or @HttpExchange

**OpenFeign (Spring Cloud OpenFeign)**
- Declarative HTTP client from Netflix OSS
- Similar to @HttpExchange conceptually but richer ecosystem (Resilience4j integration, logging, custom encoders)
- Still widely used in Spring Cloud stacks
- Case weakens in Spring 6+ with native @HttpExchange

**JDK HttpClient, Apache HttpClient 5, OkHttp**
- Low-level libraries Spring can sit on top of
- Use for specific features (HTTP/2 tuning, HTTP/3, connection pooling)

**Default pick for Spring 6+ new code**
- @HttpExchange backed by RestClient for sync
- Or WebClient for reactive
- Wrap with Resilience4j for circuit breaking, timeouts, retries
- Tune connection pool
- Propagate trace headers

**Usage examples**

*@HttpExchange*
- Define interface with @GetExchange, @PostExchange annotations
- Configure with RestClient builder
- Build via HttpServiceProxyFactory + RestClientAdapter
- Cleaner than Feign for simple cases; no external dep

*RestClient*
- Fluent: builder.baseUrl().defaultHeader()
- client.post().uri().body().retrieve().onStatus().body()
- Imperative modern sync

*WebClient*
- Reactive; Mono/Flux
- client.get().uri().retrieve().onStatus().bodyToMono().timeout()
- Use in WebFlux; can .block() in MVC (but if everywhere blocking, don't need WebClient)

*OpenFeign*
- @FeignClient(name, url); Spring Cloud discovers via Eureka/Consul
- Integrates with LoadBalancer, Resilience4j, Sleuth

**Production concerns**

*Timeouts non-negotiable*
- Connect timeout: 1 to 2s internal, 5s external
- Read timeout: 2 to 10s internal, 10 to 30s external
- Total/request timeout: overall ceiling
- Default clients often have huge or no timeouts; requests hang forever

*Connection pool tuning*
- Default pool sizes rarely fit production
- Tune: max connections per route, total max, idle timeout, evict policy
- Monitor pool saturation
- Example: Apache HttpClient 5 with PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager

*Resilience4j for circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, timeout*
- @CircuitBreaker, @Retry, @Bulkhead, @TimeLimiter annotations
- Config in application.yml: slidingWindowSize, failureRateThreshold, waitDurationInOpenState, maxAttempts, timeoutDuration
- Fallback method for graceful degradation

*Observability*
- Metrics: Micrometer auto-instruments; http.client.requests with URI, method, status, outcome
- Tracing: Spring + OpenTelemetry / Micrometer Tracing auto-propagates traceparent
- Logging: careful not to log bodies (PII/secrets); log correlation id, URL, status, duration

*Auth propagation*
- Propagate JWT / auth context for on-behalf-of-user
- Service-to-service: OAuth2 client credentials or mTLS
- ExchangeFilterFunction (WebClient), RestClient interceptors, or RequestInterceptor (Feign) to inject tokens

*MDC / tracing headers propagation*
- When switching threads, MDC can be lost
- Spring Cloud Sleuth / Micrometer Tracing handle propagation
- Verify trace IDs appear in downstream logs

*Error handling patterns*
- Don't let RestClientException bubble unfiltered; map to domain exceptions
- 4xx client error: don't retry
- 5xx server error: retry idempotent
- 429 rate limited: back off
- 503 unavailable: retry
- Idempotency keys on non-idempotent POSTs when retrying

**Trade-offs**

*RestClient vs WebClient*
- Sync RestClient: simpler debugging, stack traces, Transactional boundaries
- Reactive WebClient: non-blocking, streaming, high concurrency, backpressure
- With Project Loom, sync Tomcat + RestClient handles high concurrency efficiently
- Still pick WebClient for streaming, fully reactive pipelines, or WebFlux apps

*@HttpExchange vs Feign*
- @HttpExchange native to Spring 6; no extra dep
- Feign has deeper ecosystem (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, decoders)
- New code on Spring 6+: @HttpExchange usually wins
- Existing Spring Cloud projects: Feign entrenched

*When NOT to use declarative*
- Complex dynamic URL; computed headers per request
- Per-call ExchangeFilterFunction or interceptor
- Streaming with per-chunk logic
- Use imperative RestClient or WebClient directly

*HTTP/2 adoption*
- WebClient (Reactor Netty), RestClient (JDK HttpClient), Apache HttpClient 5 all support
- Multiplexing reduces connection overhead

*HTTP/3 (QUIC) emerging*
- Experimental; production niche

*gRPC as alternative*
- Internal microservice calls often better in gRPC: HTTP/2, Protobuf, strong types
- REST still default for public APIs

*Circuit breaker antipattern*
- Fallback that masks errors silently
- Fallback should return cached/default, queue for later, or clearly indicate failure
- Don't paper over bad dependencies; fix them

*Retry antipattern*
- Retrying non-idempotent POSTs without idempotency keys
- Retrying on client errors
- Exponential backoff + jitter; cap attempts (3 typical)

*Timeout antipattern*
- 30s default; thread pool exhaustion
- Aggressive internal timeouts
- Timeout budget accounts for retries

*Testing*
- MockWebServer (okhttp): full HTTP mock
- WireMock: classic Java HTTP mock
- MockRestServiceServer (Spring): mock client side
- Prefer real HTTP mocks over mocking RestTemplate

*Security*
- TLS for all external; validate certificates
- mTLS for service-to-service (Istio or manual)
- Secrets in Vault/Secrets Manager
- Never log tokens

**The strategic answer**
- Spring 6+ new code: @HttpExchange + RestClient (or WebClient) default
- RestTemplate only for legacy maintenance
- OpenFeign where Spring Cloud stack entrenched
- Timeouts, connection pool, Resilience4j are essential
- Observability with Micrometer and distributed tracing
- Test with MockWebServer/WireMock; not by mocking client directly
- Consider gRPC for internal service-to-service calls

questions.question: How do you use OpenFeign in Spring Cloud — @FeignClient, interceptors, error decoding, retry, and circuit breaker integration?
questions.title: OpenFeign + Spring Cloud — Production Integration
questions.direct_answer: **OpenFeign** is declarative; you define a Java interface annotated with `**@FeignClient**(name, url)` and Spring Cloud generates an HTTP proxy. Production-grade usage requires four pillars: **`RequestInterceptor`** to inject auth/tracing headers, **`ErrorDecoder`** to translate upstream errors into typed exceptions, **Resilience4j** `CircuitBreaker`/`Retry` via `@CircuitBreaker` on the Feign bean (or Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker auto-config), and explicit **`Feign.Builder` timeouts** (`connectTimeout`, `readTimeout`) because the defaults are 10s/60s — far too long. Use Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (`name = "payment-service"` with no `url`) to resolve service names via Eureka/Consul/Kubernetes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can configure OpenFeign beyond the trivial @FeignClient declaration — timeouts, auth, error mapping, retry, and circuit breaker — and whether you understand how Spring Cloud LoadBalancer integrates with Feign.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Shipping @FeignClient with default 10s/60s timeouts and no circuit breaker, so one slow downstream saturates the caller's Tomcat thread pool within minutes. Also: swallowing the Response body inside ErrorDecoder so errors arrive at the caller with no context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Feign's per-method configuration via `@FeignClient(configuration = ...)`, custom `Contract` for non-Spring MVC annotations, `RequestInterceptor` ordering, decoded-exception propagation via `ErrorDecoder`, and the Resilience4j bulkhead as a complement to the circuit breaker.

sections.title: Why OpenFeign Still Wins in Spring Cloud Stacks
sections.content:
OpenFeign turns an HTTP call into an **interface method**.
- You declare `UserClient.getUser(id)`, add `@FeignClient(name = "user-service")`, and Spring Cloud wires in a proxy that serializes arguments, adds headers, resolves the target host via LoadBalancer, executes the call, decodes the response, and maps errors.
- The same interface can be reused by tests with a fake implementation.

Against Spring 6's native `@HttpExchange`, Feign still has three durable advantages in Spring Cloud codebases:
- **Deep Spring Cloud integration** — LoadBalancer, service discovery (Eureka/Consul/Kubernetes), distributed tracing via Micrometer Tracing, and CircuitBreaker auto-config all plug in with a single starter dependency
- **Mature plugin surface** — custom `Contract`, `Encoder`, `Decoder`, `RequestInterceptor`, `ErrorDecoder`, `Retryer` — every seam is well-documented
- **Per-client configuration class** — `@FeignClient(configuration = UserClientConfig.class)` gives you a fully isolated bean graph per remote service, which `@HttpExchange` still doesn't match cleanly

The cost is the extra dependency (`spring-cloud-starter-openfeign`) and the tight coupling to Spring Cloud release trains. On a green-field Spring 6 service with no Spring Cloud, `@HttpExchange` is lighter.

sections.title: Minimal @FeignClient with Service Discovery
Per-Client Configuration — Interceptor, ErrorDecoder, Timeouts, Retryer
Resilience4j Circuit Breaker + Retry — application.yml
sections.content:
spring:
  cloud:
    openfeign:
      circuitbreaker:
        enabled: true          # auto-wrap every Feign method in a CircuitBreaker
        group:
          enabled: true        # one CB per @FeignClient name (not per method)

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payment-service:
        slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 50
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 20
        failureRateThreshold: 40          # open when >=40% of last 50 calls fail
        slowCallRateThreshold: 60
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s
        waitDurationInOpenState: 10s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
        recordExceptions:
          - com.acme.payments.PaymentUpstreamException
          - java.io.IOException
        ignoreExceptions:
          - com.acme.payments.PaymentBadRequestException
          - com.acme.payments.PaymentNotFoundException
  retry:
    instances:
      payment-service:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 200ms
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
        retryExceptions:
          - com.acme.payments.PaymentUpstreamException
          - feign.RetryableException

# fine-grained Feign tuning that survives config refresh
feign:
  client:
    config:
      payment-service:
        connectTimeout: 1000
        readTimeout: 2500
        loggerLevel: basic

sections.title: Production Anatomy — What Each Pillar Buys You
sections.content:
**`RequestInterceptor` — header injection**
- Runs before every call; modify the `RequestTemplate` (headers, query params, body)
- Use for auth tokens, tenant IDs, correlation IDs, feature flags, custom `User-Agent`
- Register via `@Bean` inside the `configuration` class so it is scoped to this client only — avoid global interceptors that leak internal tokens to every service

**`ErrorDecoder` — typed exceptions, not `FeignException`**
- Default decoder throws generic `FeignException` with the status code buried in a message
- Always read the body **before** the response is closed, and map to domain exceptions the caller can catch by type
- Return `feign.RetryableException` from transient server errors so the `Retryer` fires; throw any other exception type to short-circuit retries

**`Request.Options` — timeouts**
- Feign defaults to `connectTimeout=10s`, `readTimeout=60s` — utterly wrong for internal calls
- Set per-client via the config class or `feign.client.config.<name>.readTimeout` in YAML
- Timeout budget rule: total retry budget (`attempts × (readTimeout + backoff)`) must fit inside the caller's own SLA

**`Retryer` vs Resilience4j `@Retry`**
- Feign's own `Retryer` retries only on `RetryableException` and has no jitter — fine for simple cases
- Resilience4j `@Retry` offers exponential backoff with jitter, rich exception matching, and integrates with metrics — prefer it for anything beyond the simplest use case
- Pick one; running both stacks compound attempts silently

**`CircuitBreaker` — stop cascading failures**
- Spring Cloud OpenFeign auto-wraps every Feign method call in a `CircuitBreakerFactory` call when `spring.cloud.openfeign.circuitbreaker.enabled=true`
- Use `group.enabled=true` to get one CB per client name (saves memory vs per-method)
- Configure `failureRateThreshold`, `slowCallRateThreshold`, and `waitDurationInOpenState`; couple with the `fallback` bean on `@FeignClient`

**Service discovery**
- Omit `url`; set `name = "payment-service"` — Spring Cloud LoadBalancer resolves via Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes `EndpointSlice`
- For testing you can still override `url` via `feign.client.config.payment-service.url` property so CI uses WireMock

sections.title: Observability and Tracing for Feign
sections.content:
**Metrics**
- Micrometer auto-binds `http.client.requests` to each Feign call when `spring-boot-starter-actuator` + `micrometer-registry-*` are on the path
- Tags include `method`, `uri` (templatized), `status`, `outcome`, `clientName`
- Set up alerts on high error-rate per `clientName` before the circuit breaker opens

**Tracing**
- Micrometer Tracing injects the `traceparent` header automatically via an interceptor in `spring-cloud-starter-openfeign` — no manual work
- Each Feign call becomes a child span of the server-side span, giving you the full cross-service trace in Tempo/Jaeger/Datadog APM
- Verify by sending a test request and confirming the downstream service logs the same trace ID

**Logging**
- `feign.client.config.<name>.loggerLevel` can be `NONE`, `BASIC`, `HEADERS`, or `FULL`
- Never use `FULL` in production — it logs request/response bodies including PII and auth headers
- Prefer `BASIC` (URL, method, status, elapsed) and rely on tracing for detail

**Retry + CB visibility**
- Resilience4j exposes `resilience4j.circuitbreaker.state` and `.calls` metrics with `name` tag
- Dashboard the state gauge per client; page when a CB stays `OPEN` > 2 minutes

sections.title: When to Reach for OpenFeign — and When Not To
sections.content:
**When OpenFeign shines:**
- Spring Cloud stack with service discovery, LoadBalancer, and Resilience4j already in play
- Many remote services sharing the same interceptors, encoders, and error model — one `configuration` class per client
- Team used to declarative style; resolvers, metrics, and tracing need to be wired automatically
- Need a typed fallback bean when the circuit opens

**When `@HttpExchange` is the better pick:**
- Spring 6+ service without Spring Cloud — avoids a large dependency subtree
- Reactive pipeline where you want `WebClient` under the hood with backpressure
- Minimal set of remote services; per-client configuration class is overkill

**When imperative `RestClient`/`WebClient` wins:**
- Dynamic URLs, computed headers per call, streaming SSE, multipart uploads with progress
- You need an `ExchangeFilterFunction` per request rather than per client

**Common pitfalls:**
- Leaving default 10s/60s timeouts in place — causes thread-pool exhaustion under any upstream slowdown
- Enabling both Feign `Retryer` and Resilience4j `@Retry` — silent multiplicative attempts (3 × 3 = 9)
- Catching `FeignException` generically instead of modelling domain exceptions through `ErrorDecoder`
- Logging `FULL` request/response in production, leaking PII and bearer tokens
- Reusing a single `@FeignClient` interface for fundamentally different remotes — `configuration = ...` per remote is the idiomatic separation

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@FeignClient` + a per-client `configuration` class** is the production shape — one `RequestInterceptor`, `ErrorDecoder`, `Retryer`, and `Request.Options` per remote service
- **Always override the defaults** — 10s connect / 60s read is lethal under upstream slowdowns; budget the timeouts against your own SLA
- **`ErrorDecoder` must map to typed exceptions** — `FeignException` at the caller is an antipattern; return `RetryableException` for transient errors so the `Retryer` engages
- **Resilience4j integration** via `spring.cloud.openfeign.circuitbreaker.enabled=true` wraps every Feign method; use `group.enabled=true` for one CB per client
- **Pick one retry layer** — Feign's `Retryer` or Resilience4j `@Retry` — never both, or attempts multiply silently
- **Observability comes free** via Micrometer + Micrometer Tracing; just avoid `loggerLevel: FULL` in production to protect PII
- **Service discovery is the big win** — `name = "payment-service"` with no `url` resolves through Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (Eureka/Consul/K8s)

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
OpenFeign is still the right pick when you're already on Spring Cloud. It turns an HTTP call into an interface method, and then four pillars make it production-grade.

**Declaration and discovery**
- `@FeignClient(name = "payment-service", configuration = PaymentClientConfig.class)` — no `url`, so Spring Cloud LoadBalancer resolves the host via Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes
- The per-client configuration class scopes interceptors, error decoders, and timeouts to this one remote

**RequestInterceptor**
- Runs before every call; I inject the bearer token, tenant ID, and correlation headers here
- Keep it scoped to the configuration class so internal tokens never leak to unrelated clients

**ErrorDecoder**
- The default throws a generic `FeignException` — I always replace it with a decoder that maps 400/401/404/409/429/5xx to typed domain exceptions
- For 5xx and I/O errors I return `feign.RetryableException` so the Retryer fires; everything else short-circuits

**Timeouts**
- Feign defaults to 10s connect and 60s read, which is how one slow downstream saturates the caller's Tomcat pool
- I set `connectTimeout: 1000` and `readTimeout: 2500` for internal calls, then compute the retry budget to fit inside the caller's own SLA

**Circuit breaker + retry**
- I turn on `spring.cloud.openfeign.circuitbreaker.enabled=true` and define a Resilience4j `CircuitBreaker` per client name
- Either Feign's Retryer or Resilience4j `@Retry` — never both, or attempts multiply
- Fallback bean on `@FeignClient(fallback = ...)` for graceful degradation when the circuit opens

**Observability**
- Micrometer auto-binds `http.client.requests` by client name; Micrometer Tracing injects `traceparent` into every call
- `loggerLevel: basic` in production; never `FULL`, because it logs bodies and auth headers

**When I wouldn't use Feign**
- Green-field Spring 6 service with no Spring Cloud — `@HttpExchange` is lighter
- Reactive or streaming pipelines — use `WebClient` directly

questions.question: How do you tune Spring WebClient for production — connection pool, timeouts, backpressure, retries, and error handling?
questions.title: WebClient Production Tuning — Pool, Timeouts, Backpressure
questions.direct_answer: Production **`WebClient`** needs five explicit knobs: a **Reactor Netty `ConnectionProvider`** sized for concurrency (`maxConnections`, `pendingAcquireTimeout`), an **`HttpClient`** with `responseTimeout`, `connectTimeout`, and per-op read/write timeouts, `retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...))` restricted to idempotent calls and transient errors, `onStatus(...)` that reads the body into a typed exception before propagating, and `limitRate(n)` on response streams to apply **backpressure** to SSE/NDJSON endpoints. Wire Micrometer metrics via `.metrics()` and always call `.block()` with an explicit `.timeout(Duration)` — never rely on Netty defaults.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the five production knobs that separate a toy WebClient from a resilient one: connection pool sizing, layered timeouts, retry strategy, body-aware error handling, and backpressure on streaming responses.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a `WebClient.create()` per call — spins up a new Reactor Netty connection pool each time and leaks memory; alternately, using `retry(3)` without filtering which statuses or exceptions are retryable, so 4xx client errors retry and amplify load.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain `pendingAcquireTimeout` vs `responseTimeout`, backpressure via `limitRate`/`take`, how `onStatus` must consume the body or risk leaks, the `DataBufferUtils.release` trap, and Micrometer `.metrics()` tags including `clientName`.

sections.title: Why a Default WebClient Breaks Under Load
sections.content:
`WebClient.create()` is convenient — and dangerous. It builds a fresh Reactor Netty `ConnectionProvider` with defaults tuned for a demo, not for a service taking 5,000 requests per second: 500 max connections, no `pendingAcquireTimeout`, no response timeout, and no metrics. Under load three failure modes dominate:

- **Pool saturation** — connections leak because `onStatus` branches forget to consume the body, so the pool drains within minutes
- **Unbounded waiting** — a single slow upstream stalls every caller because there is no `responseTimeout` and the default `pendingAcquireTimeout` is effectively infinite
- **Retry storms** — naive `.retry(3)` repeats 4xx client errors and amplifies a bad request into three bad requests

A production `WebClient` is a single shared bean per logical remote, configured with an explicit pool, layered timeouts, filtered retries, typed error mapping, backpressure on streams, and Micrometer metrics. Everything else is technical debt that surfaces during an incident.

sections.title: Shared WebClient Bean — Pool, Timeouts, Metrics
Calling the Client — Status Handling, Retries, Timeouts
Backpressure on Streaming Responses (SSE / NDJSON)
The Five Production Knobs — What Each Does
sections.content:
**1. `ConnectionProvider` — the pool**
- `maxConnections` caps in-flight concurrency to this remote; size to `p99_latency × target_rps`
- `pendingAcquireTimeout` bounds how long a caller waits for a free connection — set it to **hundreds of milliseconds**, not infinity
- `maxIdleTime` + `maxLifeTime` recycle connections so NAT/firewall resets don't surface as random failures
- `evictInBackground` asynchronously prunes stale connections — costs nothing, prevents ghost connections

**2. Layered timeouts**
- `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS` — TCP handshake ceiling (1–2 s internal)
- `responseTimeout` on `HttpClient` — whole-response deadline, maps to read timeout
- `ReadTimeoutHandler` / `WriteTimeoutHandler` — per-operation handler timeouts
- `.timeout(Duration)` on the outer `Mono`/`Flux` — caller-side overall ceiling; complements (does not replace) Netty's

**3. Retries**
- `Retry.backoff(maxAttempts, initialBackoff)` is the production retry: exponential with jitter
- Always `.filter(...)` — retry only idempotent calls on transient errors (`5xx`, `TimeoutException`, `ConnectException`)
- Never retry 4xx client errors; never retry non-idempotent POSTs without an `Idempotency-Key`
- Compose with `CircuitBreakerOperator` from Resilience4j, not retries that hide a broken dependency

**4. `onStatus` with body consumption**
- Any branch of `onStatus` that does not consume the body **leaks connections** from the pool
- Always call `resp.bodyToMono(...)` (or `releaseBody()`) and map to a typed exception
- Provide `defaultIfEmpty(...)` so empty bodies don't hang the chain

**5. Backpressure on streams**
- `.limitRate(n)` — tell the server how much you are willing to pull
- `.onBackpressureBuffer(cap, onDrop, strategy)` — bounded memory with a clear drop policy
- `.flatMap(fn, concurrency)` — cap concurrent downstream fan-out
- Without these, a fast server will overwhelm a slow consumer and the heap

sections.title: Observability and Threading Traps
sections.content:
**Metrics**
- Enable `.metrics(true)` on both `ConnectionProvider` and `HttpClient` — Reactor Netty exposes `reactor.netty.connection.provider.pending.connections`, `.total.connections`, `.idle.connections`
- `WebClient` exposes `http.client.requests` with tags `method`, `uri`, `status`, `outcome`, `clientName` via `DefaultClientRequestObservationConvention`
- Alert when `pending.connections` rises — it is the earliest signal of pool exhaustion, ahead of errors

**Tracing**
- Micrometer Tracing auto-propagates `traceparent` via an `ExchangeFilterFunction` added by Spring Boot's `ObservationAutoConfiguration`
- Every outbound call becomes a child span of the caller; verify by checking downstream logs share the trace ID

**Context propagation**
- `contextWrite(Context.of(...))` is the only safe way to carry request-scoped values (tenant, user ID) across reactive operators — MDC does **not** survive Reactor's thread switches
- Use `ContextRegistry` + `Micrometer Context Propagation` to bridge MDC/Tracing automatically

**Blocking traps**
- Never call `.block()` inside a reactive pipeline — it can deadlock the shared Reactor thread pool
- If a controller is fully reactive, return `Mono`/`Flux`; reserve `.block()` for imperative callers and pair with an explicit `.timeout(Duration)`
- `BlockHound` in tests catches accidental blocking calls on reactive threads

**DataBuffer leaks**
- When using `exchangeToMono` / low-level codecs, a non-consumed body is a direct-memory leak
- Always `.bodyToMono(T)` or `releaseBody()`; `DataBufferUtils.release(buffer)` after manual handling

sections.title: Trade-offs and Anti-patterns
sections.content:
**When WebClient earns its complexity:**
- Hundreds to thousands of concurrent outbound calls — Netty's event loop outperforms thread-per-request
- Streaming — SSE, chunked, NDJSON; the blocking clients can't express backpressure
- Reactive pipelines — you already have `Mono`/`Flux` plumbing and don't want to cross the sync boundary

**When it is overkill:**
- Dozens of calls per second, simple request/response — `RestClient` with Apache HttpClient 5 is simpler, debuggable, and on Java 21 + virtual threads the concurrency gap narrows sharply
- Non-reactive team — `.flatMap` chains and operator semantics cost more learning than they save

**Common anti-patterns:**
- `WebClient.create()` per call — fresh pool per request, heap fills with orphan Netty resources
- `.retry(3)` without a filter — turns one bad 400 into three bad 400s
- No `pendingAcquireTimeout` — pool saturation stalls every caller indefinitely
- `onStatus` branch that only logs, never consumes the body — slow connection leak into pool exhaustion
- `.block()` inside an `ExchangeFilterFunction` — deadlocks the Reactor event loop
- Using `Mono.subscribeOn(Schedulers.parallel())` to "make it faster" — Reactor Netty is already on an event loop; `parallel()` is for CPU-bound work, not I/O

**Decision heuristic:**
- Streaming, backpressure, high concurrency, WebFlux → `WebClient`
- Everything else in Spring 6+ → `RestClient` or `@HttpExchange`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One shared `WebClient` bean per remote**, not `WebClient.create()` per call — each new builder spins up a Reactor Netty pool
- **`ConnectionProvider` sized explicitly** with `maxConnections`, `pendingAcquireTimeout`, `maxIdleTime`, `maxLifeTime` — defaults hide pool saturation until it's already cascading
- **Layered timeouts**: `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS` + `responseTimeout` + `ReadTimeoutHandler` + outer `.timeout(Duration)` — each protects a different failure mode
- **`onStatus(...)` must consume the body** — unconsumed responses leak connections from the pool; map to typed exceptions with `bodyToMono(ApiError.class)` and a `defaultIfEmpty`
- **Filter retries** with `Retry.backoff(...).filter(...)` — never retry 4xx client errors and never retry non-idempotent POSTs without an `Idempotency-Key`
- **Backpressure on streams** via `.limitRate(n)` + bounded `onBackpressureBuffer` — without them a fast server overwhelms the heap
- **Observability is free but must be enabled** — `.metrics(true)` on pool and `HttpClient`, `ObservationRegistry` on the `WebClient.Builder`, watch `pending.connections` as the early-warning gauge
- **Context propagation** via `contextWrite(...)` and Micrometer Context Propagation — MDC does not survive Reactor thread switches

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Production WebClient tuning comes down to five knobs, and `WebClient.create()` sets none of them.

**The connection pool**
- A shared `ConnectionProvider` per remote — sized to `p99 latency × target RPS`
- `maxConnections` caps concurrency; `pendingAcquireTimeout` bounds the wait when the pool is empty — I set it to a few hundred ms, never infinite
- `maxIdleTime` and `maxLifeTime` recycle sockets so NAT and firewall timeouts don't surface as random errors

**Layered timeouts**
- TCP connect timeout on the Netty channel option
- `responseTimeout` on the `HttpClient` — whole-response deadline
- `ReadTimeoutHandler` and `WriteTimeoutHandler` for per-op protection
- `.timeout(Duration)` on the outer Mono as the caller-side ceiling
- Four timeouts, each for a different failure mode

**Retries that don't amplify pain**
- `Retry.backoff(maxAttempts, initialBackoff)` with jitter
- Always a `.filter(...)` so only idempotent calls on transient errors retry
- Never retry 4xx, and never retry non-idempotent POSTs unless the request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
- Compose with a Resilience4j circuit breaker via `CircuitBreakerOperator` so retries don't hide a broken dependency

**`onStatus` must consume the body**
- Every branch reads `bodyToMono(ApiError.class)` and maps to a typed exception
- Forgetting to consume the body is the silent killer — connections leak from the pool until every caller blocks on `pendingAcquire`

**Backpressure for streams**
- `.limitRate(n)` for SSE and NDJSON responses
- `.onBackpressureBuffer(cap, onDrop, strategy)` to bound memory
- `flatMap(fn, concurrency)` to cap fan-out
- Without these, a fast upstream overwhelms the heap

**Observability**
- `.metrics(true)` on both the pool and the `HttpClient`
- `ObservationRegistry` on the builder gives me `http.client.requests` with a `clientName` tag
- The earliest signal of trouble is `reactor.netty.connection.provider.pending.connections` rising — it leads the error spike by a minute

**When I wouldn't reach for WebClient**
- Dozens of calls per second, simple request/response, no streaming — `RestClient` is simpler and, on Java 21 with virtual threads, nearly as concurrent
- I pick WebClient when streaming, backpressure, or reactive composition is the real requirement
